item.title: 8(a) Certification Requirements: 2026 Pass/Fail Checklist
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: 8(a) certification requirements: the $850K net worth, $400K income and $6.5M asset limits, the new social disadvantage rule, and a pass/fail checklist.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

8(a) certification requires a firm that is small under SBA size standards and at least 51% directly owned and controlled by socially and economically disadvantaged U.S. citizens. Each of those owners must have net worth of $850,000 or less, average AGI of $400,000 or less, and total assets of $6.5 million or less (13 CFR 124.104).

You also need good character and, in most cases, two full years of operating revenue (SBA). The biggest change in 2026: since September 10, 2026, no racial or ethnic group is presumed socially disadvantaged. Individual applicants now have to document discrimination against their group and self-certify that it materially harmed them (Holland & Knight).

Which option is right for you?

Choose your starting point by asking which gate you are least sure you can pass. Each row below names the first thing to check and the official page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time bidder, firm under 2 years oldCheck the two-year rule and its five-part waiver before anything else, because without a waiver you can't apply yet13 CFR 124.107
You already bid federal work every day and have tax returns showing revenueRun the three financial tests ($850K / $400K / $6.5M), then gather social disadvantage evidence13 CFR 124.104
Woman-owned firm that may fail the 8(a) social disadvantage testLook at WOSB/EDWOSB, which has no social disadvantage narrativeSBA WOSB program
Office in a distressed area, many local hiresCheck HUBZone (35% employee residency rule)SBA HUBZone
Tight budget, unsure about any gateUse free SBA and APEX Accelerator counseling before you pay anyoneapexaccelerators.us
Your application was pending in September 2026Expect it to be returned and plan to resubmit under the new evidence testUSFCR summary

One terminology note: many people search for "Certify.gov," but the current portal is MySBA Certifications at certifications.sba.gov. The old certify.sba.gov sign-in page still exists (SBA Certify).

What Is 8(a) Certification?

The SBA 8(a) Business Development program certifies small businesses owned by socially and economically disadvantaged individuals. Certified firms can win sole-source and set-aside federal contracts for up to 9 years. It is a business development program with a fixed end date, and you only get one turn: SBA calls it one-time participation per individual over a lifetime (SBA).

The most valuable benefit is the sole-source award. Agencies can give an 8(a) firm a contract directly, without competition, up to set dollar thresholds. As of October 1, 2025, the FAR inflation adjustment raised those thresholds from $4.5 million to $5.5 million for most acquisitions and from $7 million to $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes (Federal Register, Aug. 27, 2025; SmallGovCon). Above those amounts, contracts are normally competed among 8(a) firms. The exception is firms owned by Indian tribes or Alaska Native Corporations, where SBA can accept larger sole-source awards (FAR 19.805-1).

For example, a two-person IT services firm in the program could take a $3 million help-desk requirement as a sole-source award, because it falls under the $5.5 million non-manufacturing threshold. If that same requirement were $6 million, it would normally be competed among 8(a) firms instead.

You should also know the program has been under heavy scrutiny in 2026. In January, SBA suspended 1,091 participants, about 25% of the roughly 4,300 firms in the program, for missing a January 19, 2026 deadline to submit three years of financial documents (SBA news release 26-26). In March it moved to terminate more than 620 firms (SBA news release 26-34). If you join, assume SBA will ask for clean financial records and will expect them on time.

8(a) Certification Requirements (Full Eligibility Checklist)

Eligibility depends on business size, ownership and control by a disadvantaged individual, and that owner's net worth, income and assets. Every item below is pass/fail. Missing one disqualifies you even if you pass the rest.

#GatePass if…Source
1SizeThe firm is small under the SBA size standard for its primary NAICS codeSBA
2OwnershipAt least 51% is "unconditionally and directly owned" by disadvantaged U.S. citizens (no holding company; trusts only in limited cases such as revocable living trusts)13 CFR 124.105
3ControlA disadvantaged owner holds the highest officer position and works in the business full-time during normal hours13 CFR 124.106
4Social disadvantageYou have evidence of discrimination against your group and can self-certify material harm (new 2026 standard)Federal Register 2026-16370
5Net worthAdjusted net worth is $850,000 or less13 CFR 124.104
6IncomeThree-year average AGI is $400,000 or lesssame
7Total assetsFair market value of all assets is $6.5 million or lesssame
8Potential for successTwo full years of operations with operating revenue on both tax returns, or a waiver13 CFR 124.107
9Good characterNo disqualifying integrity issuesSBA
10One-time useYou have never used your disadvantaged status for another 8(a) firm, and no conflicting family-member firm existsSBA; 13 CFR 124.105

Work through the checklist in this order, because the cheapest checks come first:

  1. Look up your size standard. Find your primary NAICS code and compare your average receipts or employee count to SBA's size standard. If you fail here, nothing else matters.
  2. Read your own operating agreement or bylaws. Look for anything that gives a non-disadvantaged person veto power, supermajority votes, or the right to block decisions. Under 13 CFR 124.106, a disadvantaged owner of a corporation controls the board through 100% ownership, or 51%+ voting stock plus a board seat, provided no supermajority requirements get in the way.
  3. Run the three financial tests (next section) for each disadvantaged owner.
  4. Pull two years of business tax returns and confirm both show operating revenue.
  5. Start collecting social disadvantage evidence. It takes the longest, so begin it in parallel with steps 1–4.

Pitfall: ownership through a holding company fails the "directly owned" test. Fix: restructure so the individual holds the shares directly before you apply, and keep the transfer documents.

What Are the Net Worth, Income, and Asset Limits for 8(a)?

SBA caps adjusted net worth at $850,000, three-year average AGI at $400,000, and total assets at $6.5 million. Each cap has its own exclusions, and applicants often apply the exclusions to the wrong test (13 CFR 124.104, as of October 2026).

TestLimitExcludedNot excluded (common miss)
Net worth≤ $850,000Your ownership interest in the applicant firm; equity in your primary residence; funds in an IRA or other official retirement accountEquity in rental property, a second home, or other businesses
Income (AGI)≤ $400,000, averaged over the 3 preceding yearsPass-through income from an S corp, LLC or partnership that was reinvested in the businessSalary, distributions you took out, investment income
Total assets≤ $6.5 million fair market valueOnly qualified IRA/retirement fundsYour home and your business interest, both of which do count here

Sources: Cornell LII, 13 CFR 124.104; thresholds confirmed in Federal Register 2023-15078.

The total-assets test is the one people get wrong most easily. Your home and your company are excluded from net worth but included in total assets. For example (illustrative numbers only), an owner might have a $1.4 million home, a business valued at $4 million, a $700,000 rental property, and $500,000 in a 401(k). Net worth counts only the rental equity, which could be well under $850,000. Total assets count $1.4M + $4M + $0.7M = $6.1 million, a pass but with little room left. If the business value rises to $4.5 million, the owner fails.

Some other rules from 13 CFR 124.104 catch people out:

  • The home-equity exclusion has a carve-out. Equity that came from excessive withdrawals from the business is not excluded.
  • Retirement accounts need paperwork. You have to tell SBA the terms and restrictions of the account and certify that it is legitimate (eCFR).
  • Gifts to family within two years count against you. Assets transferred to immediate family for less than fair market value in the two years before you apply are attributed back to you. The exceptions are transfers for education, medical expenses, essential support, and customary gifts such as birthdays or graduations.
  • Your spouse submits separate financial information unless you are legally separated. SBA only counts the spouse's finances if the spouse plays a role in the business or has financially supported it.
  • The $400,000 AGI test is a rebuttable presumption, not an absolute bar. If a one-time event pushed you over, you can explain it. Expect to need documents that back up your explanation.

Fix for income spikes: if one year's AGI is high because of reinvested pass-through income, show it line by line using your K-1s and the business's retained earnings. That reinvested amount is exactly what the regulation excludes.

What Counts as 'Socially and Economically Disadvantaged' for 8(a)?

As of September 10, 2026, no group is presumed socially disadvantaged for individually owned firms. Every new individual applicant has to show discrimination against their group and self-certify that it materially harmed them. You must also pass the economic tests above. SBA published this final rule on August 11, 2026 (Federal Register 2026-16370; NASBP).

The new test has two parts (Holland & Knight; Covington):

  1. Group discrimination, backed by evidence. You show that a governmental or private entity "discriminated against, disfavored, or otherwise disadvantaged an identifiable racial, ethnic, or cultural group" that you belong to. Acceptable evidence includes government, university or corporate documents and policies, official statements, court decisions and administrative rulings, congressional findings, and "other adequate evidence."
  2. Membership and material harm, self-certified. You certify that you belong to the group and that you suffered "loss of access to or diminished opportunities related to economic advancement." The final rule says this can include being dissuaded from applying to a program because of barriers your group faces.

According to Holland & Knight's summary, the final rule clarifies that discrimination based on sex and disability can qualify. USFCR reports that the old narrative essay, the list of presumed groups, and the preponderance-of-evidence standard are gone (USFCR).

Who the change does not affect:

  • Entity-owned firms owned by Alaska Native Corporations, Community Development Corporations, Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian Organizations.
  • Current individually owned participants, who do not have to re-establish social disadvantage.

What to do now:

  1. Name the specific group you belong to.
  2. Collect published sources showing that an institution's policy or practice disadvantaged that group. Court rulings, agency findings and congressional findings carry the most weight because the rule lists them by name.
  3. Write a short factual statement connecting that discrimination to a concrete loss of economic opportunity for you. For example, you might describe a lending or bonding barrier, or a program you were steered away from. Keep it factual and avoid adjectives.
  4. Keep copies of every source with its URL and date.

Pitfall: writing a personal-hardship essay in the old style. The new rule is built around evidence of group-level discrimination, so an essay about individual setbacks alone answers the wrong question. Fix: lead with the documented institutional evidence, then add your material-harm certification. As of USFCR's September 2026 summary, SBA had not published detailed templates, so check the SBA 8(a) page for guidance before you submit.

How to Apply for 8(a) Certification on Certify.gov

You apply through MySBA Certifications at certifications.sba.gov (people often call it "Certify.gov"). Before you start, you need an active SAM.gov registration and your UEI, and SBA has 90 days to process a complete application (SBA).

  1. Identify your primary NAICS code(s). Your size standard depends on it.
  2. Register or renew in SAM.gov. MySBA Certifications needs your Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) and Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN), plus a CAGE Code if you have one (MySBA Certifications FAQ).
  3. Take the eligibility questionnaire at SBA Certifications for a preliminary read on whether 8(a) fits you.
  4. Sign in at certifications.sba.gov and choose your role: Primary Qualified Owner (PQO) if you are the disadvantaged owner, or contributor if you are someone else adding information (such as a spouse or another owner) (MySBA onboarding search summary).
  5. Claim your business by entering the UEI, CAGE Code (if applicable) and TIN. Make sure they match SAM exactly. After onboarding you land on your dashboard.
  6. Select 8(a) Business Development. The platform lets you apply for several certifications at once, such as 8(a) together with WOSB or HUBZone (FAQ).
  7. Upload documents covering ownership (operating agreement or bylaws, stock certificates), control (resumes, officer roles), finances (personal and business tax returns, personal financial statements for each disadvantaged owner and any required spouse), and your social disadvantage evidence.
  8. Submit and watch your dashboard and email. If SBA finds the application incomplete, it returns it for edits through email and in-app notifications. Add management+ucp@certify.sba.gov to your approved senders so those messages reach you (FAQ).

Common mistakes and fixes:

MistakeFix
UEI/TIN don't match SAM, so you can't claim the businessCorrect the record in SAM.gov first and wait for it to go active
Spouse's financial information missingInvite the spouse as a contributor early; their section can hold up the whole file
Personal financial statement includes the home but leaves out a rental propertyPut every asset on the statement, then apply exclusions only where 13 CFR 124.104 allows them
Missed return noticesWhitelist SBA's sender address and check the dashboard weekly

If your application was still pending on September 10, 2026, USFCR reports that SBA began returning pending individually owned applications so applicants can resubmit under the new test, with no resubmission deadline announced at the time (USFCR). When you get a returned file, rebuild the social disadvantage section first and keep your financials current.

Once you're certified, agencies will still judge you on how you present yourself. A short, specific capability statement is what contracting officers read when they consider you for a sole-source award.

Top Reasons 8(a) Applications Get Rejected

The regulations make some gates far easier to fail than others: control and ownership, missing financial documents, and the financial caps. Your business idea itself is rarely the problem. SBA doesn't publish a ranked list of denial reasons, so the list below is drawn from the rules themselves.

1. Control problems. The disadvantaged owner keeps a full-time job elsewhere, isn't the top officer, or a non-disadvantaged minority owner holds veto rights. A non-disadvantaged person also can't be paid more than the highest-ranking officer unless that's commercially reasonable (13 CFR 124.106). Fix: leave the outside job, amend the operating agreement, and document how pay is set.

2. Indirect ownership. Shares held through a holding LLC or an irrevocable trust fail the "directly owned" requirement (13 CFR 124.105). Fix: move the shares into the individual's name.

3. No two-year history and a weak waiver request. A waiver requires all five conditions: substantial management experience, technical experience, adequate capital, a record of successful contract performance, and the people, facilities and equipment to do the work (13 CFR 124.107). Fix: if you can't document all five, wait until you have two years of returns showing operating revenue.

4. Financial cap miscalculations. These include counting the home in net worth (it's excluded), leaving it out of total assets (it's included), or ignoring gifts to family in the last two years. Fix: rebuild the personal financial statement using the table above.

5. Prior use or family conflicts. If an immediate family member is using or has used disadvantaged status for another 8(a) firm, and the two firms share ownership, facilities or non-arm's-length contracts, or operate in the same industry without relevant experience, you can be blocked (13 CFR 124.105).

6. Social disadvantage evidence that answers the old question. Under the 2026 rule, personal hardship alone doesn't establish group-level discrimination.

What happens after a denial:

  • There is no reconsideration for declined applications (13 CFR 124.205).
  • Appeal to SBA's Office of Hearings and Appeals within 45 days. This is only allowed if the denial rests solely on social disadvantage, economic disadvantage, ownership, control, or a mix of those four (13 CFR 124.206). A denial based partly on anything else, such as potential for success, is final.
  • Reapply any time 90 calendar days after the final decision (13 CFR 124.207).

For example, a firm denied only because its owner works a second job at a hospital can't fix that on appeal, because the facts were true when SBA decided. The better route is to leave the job, wait 90 days, and reapply.

8(a) vs HUBZone vs WOSB: Which Certification Fits Your Business?

8(a) is for disadvantaged owners and lasts at most 9 years. HUBZone is based on where your office and employees are, and WOSB on women's ownership. Some businesses qualify for more than one, and MySBA Certifications lets you apply for several together.

8(a)HUBZoneWOSB / EDWOSB
Core test51% owned and controlled by socially and economically disadvantaged citizensPrincipal office in a HUBZone and 35%+ of employees living in a HUBZone51% owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizens; EDWOSB adds the economic limits
Financial limits$850K net worth / $400K AGI / $6.5M assetsNone on ownersEDWOSB only: $850K / $400K / $6.5M
Social disadvantage proofYes (new 2026 evidence standard)NoNo
Term9 years, one time onlyNo limit; recertify every 3 yearsOngoing with SBA certification
Key benefitSole-source up to $5.5M ($8.5M manufacturing)3% federal goal; 10% price evaluation preference in full and open competition5% federal goal; set-asides in eligible NAICS codes
Official page8(a)HUBZoneWOSB

Here's how to choose. If you pass the 8(a) financial caps but expect trouble with the new social disadvantage evidence, look at EDWOSB if you're a woman owner, since it uses the same financial limits without the social disadvantage test. If your office is already in a HUBZone, that certification doesn't run out after 9 years. WOSB set-asides only apply in NAICS codes where SBA has found women-owned firms underrepresented, so check the eligible NAICS list before counting on that program.

None of these programs replaces ordinary small business set-asides, which don't require any special certification. Our total vs partial set-aside checklist explains how those are structured.

How Long Does 8(a) Certification Last and What Happens After 9 Years?

8(a) certification lasts a maximum of nine years, starting from the date of SBA's approval letter. It is split into a 4-year developmental stage and a 5-year transitional stage, and when it ends you graduate and lose 8(a) benefits (13 CFR 124.2; SBA).

The term can only end early through termination, early graduation (including voluntary early graduation), or voluntary withdrawal (13 CFR 124.2). Staying in requires an annual review showing continuing eligibility (SBA). The 2026 suspensions showed what happens when firms don't produce records on request (SBA 26-26).

How to use the nine years:

  1. Years 1–4 (developmental): win your first sole-source awards, build past performance, and track every agency contact.
  2. Years 5–9 (transitional): move toward competitive work, and answer sources sought notices as a small business, not only as an 8(a) firm.
  3. Before graduating: decide whether HUBZone, WOSB or ordinary small business set-asides will carry you once 8(a) ends.
  4. Every year: keep three years of business and personal financial records ready to hand over.

Next steps

You can check most of the 8(a) gates yourself today, and free help is available if a gate is unclear.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Fill out a personal financial statement for each disadvantaged owner and run all three tests from the table above: $850K net worth, $400K average AGI, $6.5M total assets.
  2. Confirm your SAM.gov registration is active and that your UEI, CAGE and TIN match, then take the eligibility questionnaire at SBA Certifications.
  3. Start a folder for social disadvantage evidence, and record each court ruling, agency finding or policy document with its URL and date.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) are funded by the Department of Defense and offer one-on-one certification guidance at no cost (as of October 2026; check the official page). There are more than 90 centers and 300+ local offices, and you can find yours at apexaccelerators.us (SupplierDiversity.com overview). They suit first-time applicants who need someone to review a file. They are less suited to anyone facing an OHA appeal, because APEX counselors give guidance, not legal representation, and their help is not an SBA eligibility decision.
  • SBA's own help line is certifications@sba.gov or 866-SBA-HELP (866-722-4357) for portal and process questions, also free (as of October 2026; check the official page) (SBA HUBZone page). Don't expect it to coach you on your evidence strategy.
  • A government contracts attorney makes sense if your file has ownership or control complications, or if you're within the 45-day appeal window. Fees vary by firm and there is no official rate, so ask for a fixed quote. If your case is simple and your financials pass easily, you probably don't need one.

FAQ

What is 8(a) certification used for in federal contracting?

It lets agencies award contracts to your firm without competition, up to $5.5 million for most acquisitions and $8.5 million for manufacturing (as of October 2025). It also lets you compete for contracts set aside only for 8(a) firms. The certification lasts up to nine years and includes SBA business development support (FAR inflation adjustment).

What is the net worth limit to qualify for 8(a) certification?

The limit is $850,000 in personal net worth for each disadvantaged owner. Your ownership interest in the applicant firm, equity in your primary residence, and funds in official retirement accounts are excluded. Assets you gave to immediate family below fair market value in the past two years can be counted back against you (13 CFR 124.104).

How long does the 8(a) certification application take to process?

SBA says it has 90 days to process a complete application (SBA). The clock effectively restarts if SBA returns your file as incomplete. Applications pending on September 10, 2026 were returned for resubmission under the new social disadvantage rule, so those applicants are starting again.

Can a business be both 8(a) and WOSB certified?

Yes. A woman-owned firm that meets both programs' requirements can hold both, and MySBA Certifications allows several certifications through one application (FAQ). EDWOSB uses the same $850K / $400K / $6.5M financial limits as 8(a) but doesn't require the social disadvantage showing.

item.title: Sources Sought Notice: 5-Step Response Template (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How to respond to a sources sought notice: find it on SAM.gov, fill a 5-step response template, attach your capability statement and do the deadline math.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

A sources sought notice is a market research announcement that a federal agency posts on SAM.gov before it writes a solicitation. The agency wants to know which businesses can do the work and whether enough small businesses exist to set the contract aside. You respond with a short, tailored letter and your capability statement, sent to the contracting officer before the posted response date. Nothing is awarded from these responses, but they can decide whether the later contract is open only to small businesses.

Which option is right for you?

Your starting point depends on what you already have: a SAM.gov registration, a capability statement, and time to tailor each response.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, not yet registered in SAM.govGet your entity registration active, then practice by reading 3-5 live sources sought notices in your NAICS codeSAM.gov → Contract Opportunities search
Registered, no capability statement yetBuild a one-page capability statement before you respond to anything. Agencies often ask for one by name/capability-statement-example-5-sections-buyers-read-first/
Using this for daily business developmentA saved SAM.gov search filtered to Sources Sought + your NAICS codes, checked on a fixed scheduleSAM.gov saved searches (how saved searches with Notify work)
Tight budget, want a human reviewA free APEX Accelerator counselor (services are free or nominal cost)Your local APEX Accelerator
Unsure whether the work will be a total or partial set-asideRead up on set-aside types before you write, so you know what your response can affect/total-vs-partial-small-business-set-aside-2026-checklist/

One line on each: beginners lose the most time by responding before registration is active. Daily users get the most out of a saved search because notices can close in under two weeks. Budget-limited firms can get feedback for free through APEX before paying a consultant.

What Is a Sources Sought Notice?

A sources sought notice (SSN) is a market research tool agencies use to identify capable businesses before deciding how to structure a solicitation. It is not a request for proposals, and it guarantees no future contract. On SAM.gov it is its own notice type. In the official Opportunities API it is coded "r" and labeled "Sources Sought", next to types like Presolicitation ("p"), Solicitation ("o"), and Combined Synopsis/Solicitation ("k") (GSA Opportunities API).

The legal basis is market research under FAR Part 10, and the 2025-2026 rewrite of the FAR changed that part. The older FAR 10.002(b)(2) listed specific techniques. One was "publishing formal requests for information in appropriate technical or scientific journals or business publications" (48 CFR 10.002, Cornell LII). Under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO), Part 10 is much shorter. The new 10.001 requires market research before soliciting offers above the simplified acquisition threshold. It tells agencies to have "responsible and constructive exchanges with industry" and to ask for no more than the "minimum information necessary" (Acquisition.gov, FAR Overhaul Part 10). The rewrite also removed the list of techniques and the small business references from Part 10 (PilieroMazza).

As of October 2026, the RFO text works through agency class deviations while formal rulemaking continues. The FAR Council published a second batch of proposed rules on September 18, 2026, and comments closed October 19, 2026 (Nixon Peabody; SBA Office of Advocacy). In practice, the citation printed in the notice you're reading may be either the old or the new number. Both describe the same activity.

For example, a notice might be titled "Sources Sought – Janitorial Services, Building 12" under NAICS 561720. It would describe the scope, list four or five questions, ask for a capability statement of no more than 5 pages, and give a response date. That format is typical, but each agency writes its own.

What Is the Purpose of a Sources Sought Notice?

Agencies post SSNs to measure industry interest, check the NAICS code and size standard, and decide whether a set-aside is feasible. The answers feed a contracting officer's decision that has real legal weight.

The main decision is the Rule of Two. Under RFO FAR 19.104-1(a), a contract above the micro-purchase threshold must be set aside for small business if there is a reasonable expectation of offers "from two or more responsible small business concerns" that are "competitive in terms of fair market prices, quality, and delivery" (Acquisition.gov, FAR Overhaul Part 19). SBA states it plainly: if at least two small businesses could do the work for a fair price, the contract should be set aside for small businesses (SBA, guidance for contracting officials).

SBA also tells contracting officers how to write these notices. They should encourage targeted small business categories (HUBZone, 8(a), women-owned, and others) to respond, "ask only for key pieces of information you need to make the set-aside determination," and include a page limit (SBA). This tells you how your response will be read. The reader is checking capability and status against a decision. They are not scoring marketing copy.

Silence counts against you. In CORE DC, LLC v. United States, a published Court of Federal Claims decision dated August 27, 2026, the court upheld an agency's choice not to set aside a procurement. It noted that "an agency may rationally conclude a non-responding firm is unlikely to submit a proposal" (Government Contracts Legal Forum). In that case, the agency judged the four small businesses that did respond on a specific practical question: whether each could identify an available, properly zoned facility. Generic answers would not have passed that test.

Pitfalls to avoid:

  • Assuming someone else will respond. If you're one of only two capable small firms and you stay quiet, the set-aside may not happen.
  • Responding to everything. A 2019 Air Force vendor guide warns that sending a generic line card for work you can't do builds a negative image with the agency (summarized by Coley GSA). Respond only where you can do the work, either as a prime or with named teaming partners.
  • Ignoring the NAICS code. If the agency picked a code whose size standard excludes you, the SSN response is the place to say so, with reasons.

How to Respond to a Sources Sought Notice

A strong response confirms your socioeconomic status, ties your capability to the stated requirement, and arrives before the deadline. Miss any one of these and you may not be counted. These five steps assume your SAM.gov registration is active.

Step 1: Qualify the notice (15 minutes)

Open the notice on SAM.gov and read these fields first:

  1. NAICS Code and the size standard it implies. Check that you're small under that code.
  2. Set Aside field. On an SSN it's often blank, because the agency hasn't decided yet.
  3. Response Date and its time zone.
  4. Attachments/Links. The statement of work, questionnaire, or draft performance work statement is usually attached here, not in the description.
  5. Contact Information. The named contracting officer or specialist, and the email address responses go to.

Decision rule: respond if you could perform at least the core work yourself, or with a teaming partner you can name. If you can't, skip it.

Step 2: Copy the agency's questions into your draft

Paste every question or requested item from the notice into a blank document, in the agency's order and numbering. Answer directly below each one. This mirroring approach is widely recommended (GovCon Today), and it fits SBA's guidance that agencies ask only for what they need to make the set-aside call.

Step 3: Write the response letter (use the template below)

Keep to the page limit. If none is stated, 2-5 pages plus a one-page capability statement is a reasonable size, and that is a judgment call, not a rule. Put your status claims (small under the stated NAICS, plus 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB, or EDWOSB if you hold them) in the first half page.

Step 4: Attach a tailored capability statement

Change the core competencies and past performance on your standard capability statement so they match this scope, then save it as a PDF. Our guide /capability-statement-example-5-sections-buyers-read-first/ explains which sections buyers read first.

Step 5: Submit and confirm

Email (or upload, if the notice names a portal) to the exact address listed. Use the notice ID and title in the subject line, for example: Response to Sources Sought W912XX-26-R-0000 – Janitorial Services – [Company Name]. Save a copy of the sent email with its timestamp, and request a read receipt if your email client supports it.

Common mistakes and fixes:

MistakeFix
Sending a generic brochureAnswer the agency's numbered questions first, then attach the capability statement
Missing UEI or CAGEPut both in the header of page 1
Claiming a certification you don't holdClaim only statuses shown in SAM.gov or SBA certification records
Asking "please send us the RFP"Not needed. Watch SAM.gov yourself (see the last section)
Including pricing when none was requestedLeave it out unless the notice asks for a rough order of magnitude

Sources Sought Notice Template: What to Include

A usable template covers company identification, NAICS and size status, relevant past performance, direct answers to the agency's questions, and a tailored capability statement attached as a PDF. Below is a fill-in layout. The field list draws on common practice (GovCon Today; Coley GSA), and the order puts the set-aside facts where the reader looks first.

[Company letterhead]

Date: [MM/DD/YYYY]
To: [Contracting Officer name], [Agency/Office]
Via: [email address exactly as listed in the notice]
Re: Response to Sources Sought [Notice ID] – [Notice Title]

1. COMPANY IDENTIFICATION
   Legal name: [as registered in SAM.gov]
   UEI: [12 characters]    CAGE: [5 characters]
   Address: [ ]
   Point of contact: [name, title, phone, email]

2. SIZE AND SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS
   Small under NAICS [code] (size standard: [$X million / X employees])
   Certifications: [8(a) / HUBZone / SDVOSB / WOSB / EDWOSB / none]
   Intended role: [Prime / Prime with teaming partner: name, UEI / Subcontractor]

3. ANSWERS TO THE AGENCY'S QUESTIONS
   Q1 [copied text] -> Answer
   Q2 [copied text] -> Answer
   ...

4. RELEVANT PAST PERFORMANCE (2-3 examples)
   Customer | Contract no. | Value | Period | Scope match | Reference contact

5. RECOMMENDATIONS (optional, short)
   e.g., NAICS code fit, set-aside recommendation, unclear requirements

Attachment: Capability Statement (PDF, 1 page)

How each block maps to what the agency is deciding:

Template blockAgency decision it supportsCommon gap
1. IdentificationCan the CO verify you in SAM.gov and the Small Business Search (which SBA says COs are required to use)?UEI missing or the name doesn't match SAM
2. Size and statusRule of Two count; which set-aside type appliesStatus claimed under the wrong NAICS
3. AnswersIs the firm "responsible" and capable for this scope?Answers hidden in long narrative
4. Past performanceQuality and delivery leg of the Rule of TwoProjects with no scope or size match
5. RecommendationsNAICS and acquisition strategyPushing for a sole-source without a basis

Keep Section 5 short. An example of a useful recommendation: "The notice lists NAICS 541512. The described work is mostly help-desk support, which may fit 541519. Both carry the same size standard, so either supports a small business set-aside." Before you write something like that, check the actual size standards in SBA's table.

Your Small Business Search profile also matters, because a CO may check it alongside your response. SBA advises keeping it complete with certifications, a capabilities narrative, keywords, NAICS codes, and performance history (SBA).

Sources Sought Notice vs RFI: What's the Difference?

Both are pre-solicitation exchanges with industry. An RFI usually asks for technical, pricing, or planning input to shape the requirement. An SSN usually screens vendors for capability and socioeconomic status for the set-aside decision. In practice the line blurs. Agencies sometimes post a "Sources Sought/RFI" under one notice type, so read the questions rather than the label.

The regulation is in FAR Part 15. Under the older FAR 15.201(e), RFIs "may be used when the Government does not presently intend to award a contract" but wants price, delivery, market, or capability information for planning. Responses are not offers, and no format is required (48 CFR 15.201, Cornell LII). The RFO renumbers this to 15.101(c), which keeps the rule that the RFI must say the Government won't pay for information or treat responses as offers. RFO 15.101(e) adds an advisory multistep process. In that process, agencies invite capability information and then tell respondents whether they're viable competitors, without blocking them from competing (Acquisition.gov, FAR Overhaul Part 15).

Sources Sought NoticeRequest for Information (RFI)
SAM.gov notice typeSources Sought (API code "r")Often posted as Sources Sought or Special Notice ("s")
Main questionWho can do this, and are they small?What should we buy, and how is it priced and delivered?
FeedsRule of Two / set-aside decision (FAR 19.104-1)Requirements, acquisition strategy
Pricing asked?Usually notSometimes (rough order of magnitude)
Your priorityStatus + capability proofUseful technical input that also shows you know the work
Binding?NoNo (FAR 15.201(e); RFO 15.101(c))

If a notice asks both kinds of question, answer the status and capability items first. Those are what keep you in the count.

What Does 'Sources Sought Notice Only' Mean?

"Sources sought only" means no solicitation exists yet. Responding doesn't put you on a bidders list, and nobody is required to notify you when the solicitation posts. Agencies use the phrase, often with "This is not a request for proposals," to make the status unmistakable.

What it does not mean:

  • It doesn't mean the work is reserved for respondents. When the solicitation comes out, any eligible firm can compete, whether or not it answered the SSN.
  • It doesn't mean you'll be contacted. RFI-type notices must say the Government won't pay for the information or treat responses as offers (Acquisition.gov, FAR Overhaul Part 15). No rule promises you a follow-up.
  • It doesn't mean you need an interested vendors list instead. Some SAM.gov notices let vendors add themselves to an Interested Vendors List when the posting agency has turned that feature on (GovCon Chamber). Adding yourself there is separate from answering the SSN and doesn't replace the emailed response.

For example, if an SSN closes in March and the solicitation posts in July under a new notice ID, you'll only see it if you're watching your saved search or following related notices. The SAM.gov data model links sources sought notices to later presolicitation, solicitation, and award notices (GSA Opportunities API), but you still have to check.

How to Calculate Your Sources Sought Notice Deadline

Deadlines appear as a specific date and time in a named time zone on SAM.gov. Convert to your local time, then set an internal deadline 2-3 business days earlier. The Opportunities API stores this as a response timestamp plus a separate responseTz value, such as America/New_York (GSA Opportunities API). The time zone is part of the deadline, not a footnote. The RFO Part 10 text sets no minimum response period for market research (Acquisition.gov), so windows vary by notice and can be short.

Deadline math, step by step:

  1. Copy the Response Date exactly, including the time and time zone.
  2. Convert it to your local time zone. Watch daylight saving time. In 2026, DST ends Sunday, November 1, so "ET" before that date means EDT (UTC-4) and after it means EST (UTC-5).
  3. Count back business days, skipping weekends and federal holidays. Veterans Day (November 11) and Thanksgiving (November 26, 2026) fall in this window.
  4. Set your internal deadline: final PDF approved 2 business days before the cutoff, sent 1 business day before.
  5. Check the notice again 48 hours before your internal deadline for amendments. An amended notice can change the date or add questions.

Worked example (sample values): a notice posted Wednesday, October 21, 2026, lists a Response Date of Wednesday, November 4, 2026, 2:00 PM ET, and you're in California.

ItemValue
Agency cutoffWed Nov 4, 2:00 PM EST (after DST ended Nov 1)
Your local cutoffWed Nov 4, 11:00 AM PST
Calendar days available14
Final draft approvedMon Nov 2 (2 business days before)
SendTue Nov 3, morning
Amendment checkFri Oct 30

Pitfalls: reading "2:00 PM" as your local time, sending at 1:58 PM and hitting an attachment size bounce, or missing an amendment that moved the date earlier. After the response date, notices are typically archived 15 or 30 days later, or on a custom date the agency sets. Archived notices stay searchable but are inactive (GSA Opportunities API).

How to Find Sources Sought Notices on SAM.gov

Use SAM.gov's Contract Opportunities search and set Notice Type to Sources Sought. Then narrow by your NAICS code and filter on response date so only open notices show. SAM.gov is where agencies post opportunities over $25,000 and also where they release RFIs and sources sought notices (USDS TechFAR Hub).

Steps (labels as they appear in the search filters, per Winvale and GovCon Chamber):

  1. Go to SAM.gov, sign in, and choose Contract Opportunities as the search domain.
  2. In the left filter panel, open Notice Type and check Sources Sought. Consider adding Special Notice, because some agencies post market research there.
  3. Under the product/service filters, enter your primary NAICS code. Add related NAICS and PSC codes that match your past performance.
  4. Expand Dates and set Response/Date Offers Due to today or later, so closed notices drop out.
  5. Optional: use Set Aside only on solicitations. On SSNs the field is often empty, so filtering by it hides relevant notices.
  6. Sort by response date and save the search. Saved searches for Contract Opportunities offer a Notify option for new matches (DEV Community walkthrough).

Example search set (sample values): Notice Type = Sources Sought + Special Notice, NAICS = 561720 and 561790, Response/Date Offers Due = on or after 10/21/2026, keyword left blank. Try keywords only after the NAICS filter, because titles vary ("custodial" vs "janitorial").

Limitation: SAM.gov's search depends on how the contracting officer coded the notice. A miscoded NAICS will hide it from a strict filter, so run a broader keyword search once a week as a backstop. Paid aggregators exist, but they draw on the same SAM.gov data. They are not for first-time bidders who haven't yet learned the free filters, and their prices change (check each vendor's official page).

Next steps

You can do the next three actions yourself today, and free counseling exists if you want a second pair of eyes.

DIY today:

  1. Build the saved search from the previous section and open the three notices closing soonest.
  2. Copy the template above into a document, fill in sections 1 and 2 (identification and status) once, and reuse them for every response.
  3. Update your capability statement and Small Business Search profile so what you claim matches what the CO can verify.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) are funded through the DoD Office of Small Business Programs. They offer counseling free or at nominal cost, including bid and proposal review and capability statement help (LaGuardia APEX Accelerator). Good for first-time bidders who want feedback. Less useful if you need someone to write and submit responses for you on a deadline, since counselors advise rather than ghostwrite. Free as of October 2026; check your local center.
  • Paid proposal consultants or GovCon writing firms can draft responses for you. They suit firms with steady notice volume and no in-house writer. They're a poor fit if you're still testing whether federal work suits you. Fees vary widely by firm and scope, so ask for a written quote and check the firm's official pricing page.

Related guides on Set-Aside Brief:

  • /capability-statement-example-5-sections-buyers-read-first/: what to put in the PDF you attach.
  • /total-vs-partial-small-business-set-aside-2026-checklist/: what your response may lead to.

FAQ

What is sources sought?

"Sources sought" is a federal market research notice in which an agency asks businesses to say whether they can do a planned piece of work. It appears as its own notice type on SAM.gov. Responses help the contracting officer decide on a set-aside, the NAICS code, and the acquisition approach. It is not a solicitation, and nothing is awarded from it.

What is a sources sought announcement?

It's another name for a sources sought notice. SBA uses the term "sources sought announcement" in its guidance to contracting officers (SBA). Some agencies call it a sources sought synopsis. Respond the same way under any of these names.

What is the sources sought notice FAR reference?

Market research falls under FAR Part 10. The pre-overhaul technique list was in FAR 10.002(b)(2), and the RFO version puts the requirements in 10.001. Set-aside decisions that use SSN responses fall under FAR 19.104-1 in the RFO text. RFI rules are in FAR 15.201(e), renumbered 15.101(c) in the RFO.

What does SSN mean in federal contracting?

In federal contracting, SSN usually means "sources sought notice," not Social Security number. Context tells you which. A SAM.gov notice titled "SSN" or "Sources Sought" is the market research notice described here.

item.title: Total vs Partial Small Business Set Aside: 2026 Checklist
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Total vs partial small business set aside explained: FAR rule of two, 50% subcontracting limits, HUBZone price rules, and a step-by-step bid checklist.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

A total small business set-aside reserves the whole contract for small businesses, so large companies can't bid at all. A partial small business set-aside splits the requirement into two parts. One part is reserved for small businesses, and the other part is open to everyone, large firms included. Your bid strategy depends on which part you can win and how much of the work you can do with your own staff. Under the subcontracting limits, a services prime can pay non-similarly situated subcontractors no more than 50% of what the government pays it (FAR 52.219-14).

One thing that often confuses people: current FAR text gives small businesses no general price evaluation preference on partial set-asides. The only small-business price preference in FAR Part 19 is the 10% HUBZone preference, and it applies in full and open competition (FAR 19.1307). The sections below show what this means for your bid.

Which option is right for you?

Start with the notice type that matches where your business is now, then open the official page listed in the table.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, first federal bid, no certificationsTotal Small Business Set-Aside (code SBA). Only small firms compete, and self-certification in SAM.gov is enoughSAM.gov Contract Opportunities filtered by Set Aside
You already deliver this work every day and can do most of it with your own staffBoth types. On a partial set-aside, bid on both portions if the solicitation allows itThe solicitation's Section B line items and the Notice of Partial Small Business Set-Aside clause, FAR 52.219-7
Tight budget and a small team that will need subcontractorsA total set-aside where your share of the work clears the 50%/85%/75% limit, or a partial set-aside where the reserved portion is small enough to staff yourselfFAR 52.219-14, Limitations on Subcontracting
Certified HUBZone firmUnrestricted competitions and the non-set-aside portion of partial set-asides, where the 10% preference can helpFAR 19.1307
Not sure you're "small" for this jobCheck your size first and don't bid yetSBA Size Standards Tool

Here's why. Total set-asides are the simplest place to start because the competition and the rules are uniform across the whole contract. Partial set-asides reward firms that can scale, since you can win the reserved portion, the open portion, or both. Your subcontracting math decides whether either one is realistic for you.

A note on FAR section numbers in 2026

Older articles say "FAR 19.502-2" and "FAR 19.502-3". You'll now also see "19.104-1" and "19.104-2", and the reason is the FAR overhaul. The codified FAR on acquisition.gov still contains subpart 19.5. Under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul, though, agencies have issued class deviations that move total set-aside rules to 19.104-1 and combine both kinds of partial set-aside rules into 19.104-2 (Acquisition.gov FAR Overhaul Part 19; NASA deviation memo). As of October 2026, formal rulemaking for Part 19 had not been finalized (Lohfeld Consulting). The substance is largely the same. Always cite the clause numbers printed in your solicitation.

What Is a Total Small Business Set-Aside? (FAR 19.5 Definition)

A total set-aside reserves the entire acquisition for small businesses when the rule of two is met, and no large business can compete. In the rule of two, the contracting officer expects at least two responsible small businesses to submit offers that are competitive on fair market price, quality and delivery (FAR 19.502-2).

The codified rule has two dollar tiers:

  • Above the micro-purchase threshold, up to the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT): the acquisition is set aside automatically unless the contracting officer finds no reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses. If only one acceptable small business offer arrives, the CO should award to that firm. If none arrive, the set-aside is withdrawn and the requirement is resolicited on an unrestricted basis (FAR 19.502-2).
  • Above the SAT: the CO "shall set aside" the acquisition when the rule-of-two expectation exists. Past acquisition history and market research count, but they aren't the only factors (FAR 19.502-2).

As of October 2026, the micro-purchase threshold is $15,000 and the SAT is $350,000. Both were raised on October 1, 2025, from $10,000 and $250,000 (Pillsbury summary of the FAR inflation adjustment; check the FAR 2.101 definitions for current values). The overhaul version states the rule as applying to contracts "above the micro-purchase threshold" (FAR Overhaul Part 19).

Example (illustrative): an agency needs janitorial services for one building for $600,000 a year. Market research turns up five small janitorial firms that had similar contracts. The CO sets the whole requirement aside. On SAM.gov the notice shows "Total Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5)", which is set-aside code SBA in the SAM.gov Opportunities API.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: assuming you're small because you're small in general. Fix: size is measured against the NAICS code in the solicitation as of the date you submit your initial offer with price (13 CFR 121.404).
  • Pitfall: treating a total set-aside as a chance to win and then hand most of the work to a large partner. Fix: the limitations on subcontracting still apply. See the 51% rule section below.

What Is a Partial Small Business Set-Aside?

A partial set-aside reserves one or more distinct portions of a requirement for small businesses and leaves the rest open to all offerors. COs use it when a total set-aside isn't appropriate but part of the work still passes the rule of two (FAR 19.502-3).

Under codified FAR 19.502-3(a), the CO shall partially set aside when all of the following are true:

  1. Market research shows a total set-aside isn't appropriate.
  2. The requirement can be split into distinct portions.
  3. The acquisition isn't using simplified acquisition procedures.
  4. Two or more responsible small businesses are reasonably expected to offer competitively on the set-aside portion.
  5. The program eligibility requirements apply.
  6. The result won't be a multiple-award contract. Multiple-award partial set-asides were in 19.502-4 and are now combined into 19.104-2 under the overhaul.

The codified text also excludes construction from partial set-asides (FAR 19.502-3). The solicitation has to say which portions are set aside and which aren't, and how to submit offers for each one (FAR 19.502-3(b)–(c)).

Example (illustrative): a supply solicitation has 10 contract line items (CLINs). CLINs 0001–0006 are high-volume items that only a few large manufacturers can supply at scale. CLINs 0007–0010 are low-volume items that several small distributors already sell. The CO might leave 0001–0006 unrestricted and set aside 0007–0010. On SAM.gov the notice appears as "Partial Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5)", code SBP (SAM.gov Opportunities API).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: pricing only the set-aside CLINs because you assume the unrestricted portion is out of reach. Fix: the FAR 52.219-7 clause lets small businesses compete for both portions, either with separate offers or one combined offer. Decide on purpose instead of by habit.
  • Pitfall: skipping Section L (or the instructions to offerors). Fix: the CO must tell you how to submit for each portion. If you use the wrong format, a good price can be thrown out.

Total vs Partial Set-Aside: Side-by-Side Comparison

The main differences are who can compete on each part, how the requirement is divided, and which rules your offer must meet. This table shows them side by side.

FeatureTotal small business set-asidePartial small business set-aside
Who can bidSmall businesses only, on everythingSmall businesses only on the reserved portion; anyone on the non-reserved portion
SAM.gov label / codeTotal Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5) / SBAPartial Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5) / SBP
TriggerRule of two for the whole acquisitionTotal set-aside not appropriate, requirement divisible, rule of two for the reserved portion
Dollar rangeAbove $15,000 micro-purchase threshold (as of Oct 2026)Not used under simplified acquisition procedures (codified 19.502-3(a)(3))
ConstructionAllowedExcluded in codified FAR 19.502-3(a)
Large firm offer on the reserved partNot allowedRejected as nonresponsive on the set-aside portion
Limitations on subcontracting (52.219-14)Applies when the contract exceeds the SAT, per the FAR clause prescriptionApplies when any set-aside portion exceeds the SAT (FAR Overhaul Part 19)
HUBZone 10% preferenceNot applicable (not full and open)Can matter on the non-reserved, full-and-open portion; check the clauses
What happens if no acceptable small offers arriveWithdraw and resolicit unrestricted (at or below SAT)Depends on the solicitation; the CO can withdraw the set-aside (FAR 19.506)

Sources for the rows: FAR 19.502-2, FAR 19.502-3, FAR 52.219-7, FAR 19.1307.

What Is the 51% Rule for Small Business Set-Asides?

The "51% rule" is an old nickname. Today's rule caps how much of the contract money you can pay to subcontractors that aren't similarly situated. For services and supplies the cap is 50% (13 CFR 125.6; FAR 52.219-14, Oct 2022 version).

The rule measures money paid out, not hours worked. The current limits are:

Contract typeMaximum you may pay to non-similarly situated subcontractorsWhat's excluded from the calculation
Services (except construction)50% of the amount the government pays youSome other direct costs, such as airline travel or cloud computing, when they aren't the main purpose of the buy (13 CFR 125.6)
Supplies / products50%Cost of materials
General construction85%Cost of materials
Special trade construction75%Cost of materials

A similarly situated entity is a first-tier subcontractor that has the same small business program status as you and is small under the NAICS code assigned to the subcontract. Work it performs with its own employees doesn't count against your cap (FAR 52.219-14).

Example (illustrative): you win a $1,000,000 total small business set-aside for IT help desk services. You plan to pay $300,000 to a large company for tier-2 support and $250,000 to another small business for on-site staff. Only the $300,000 counts toward the cap, so you're at 30%, well under 50%. Now suppose the "small" partner is actually large under the subcontract's NAICS code. Then you're at 55%, and you're out of compliance.

Compliance is generally measured over the base term and then over each option period separately (13 CFR 125.6(c)). The penalty is steep: the greater of $500,000 or the amount paid to subcontractors above the allowed level (13 CFR 125.6).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: checking compliance only for the whole contract. Fix: run the numbers separately for the base year and for each option year in your pricing spreadsheet.
  • Pitfall: relying on a teaming partner's word that it's small. Fix: look up its SAM.gov entity record and check its size under the subcontract's NAICS code. Primes may usually rely on a subcontractor's self-certification unless they have reason to doubt it (13 CFR 121.404), but the risk is still yours if the certification turns out to be wrong.
  • Pitfall: if you're a nonmanufacturer on a supply set-aside, offering a large manufacturer's product without a waiver. Fix: the nonmanufacturer rule generally requires products from small business manufacturers unless a waiver applies (13 CFR 125.6(a)(2)).

How Does the Rule of Two Determine Which Set-Aside Applies?

The contracting officer runs market research to see whether two or more responsible small businesses can perform at a fair price. That result decides whether the buy is a total set-aside, a partial set-aside, or unrestricted (FAR 19.502-2; FAR Overhaul 19.104-1).

From the CO's side, the decision usually goes like this:

  1. Market research. The CO reviews past awards, searches SAM.gov entity data, and often posts a Sources Sought or RFI notice on SAM.gov.
  2. Rule of two for the whole requirement. If two or more capable small businesses are expected to offer, the result is a total set-aside. The overhaul text keeps this as a "must."
  3. If that fails, check for divisible portions. If some portions pass the rule of two and the codified 19.502-3 conditions are met (not construction, not simplified procedures), the result is a partial set-aside.
  4. If nothing passes, the buy goes unrestricted, and the CO documents why it wasn't set aside. SAM.gov may label it "No Set aside used". SBA can recommend a set-aside, and a CO who rejects that recommendation has to follow a set procedure (FAR Overhaul Part 19).

What this means for you: step 1 is where you can affect the outcome. If you answer a Sources Sought notice with a clear capability statement showing relevant past performance, you become one of the "two" the CO is counting. A short, specific response does more than a brochure. The capability statement example guide covers the five sections buyers read first.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall: ignoring Sources Sought notices because "they aren't real contracts." Fix: treat them as the stage where the set-aside type is decided, and answer the questions exactly as the notice asks.
  • Pitfall: answering an RFI without saying whether you would bid as a prime. Fix: state your size under the stated NAICS code, whether you would prime, and what portion of the work you would do yourself.

What Is the Price Evaluation Preference in Partial Set-Asides?

Current FAR text gives small businesses no general price evaluation preference on either portion of a partial set-aside. Small offers on the set-aside portion compete only against other small offers. The only Part 19 price preference is the 10% HUBZone factor, and it applies in full and open competition (FAR 52.219-7; FAR 19.1307).

Some guides say small businesses get a price adjustment on the open portion of a partial set-aside. The official text doesn't support that. Here's what does apply:

  • Set-aside portion: you're evaluated only against other small businesses. Large business offers on this portion are rejected as nonresponsive (FAR 19.502-3(d)).
  • Non-set-aside portion: this is open competition. If you're a certified HUBZone firm and the solicitation includes FAR 52.219-4, the CO adds 10% to the prices of offerors that aren't HUBZone or otherwise successful small business offerors. The adjustment is for evaluation only, and you're paid your actual price (FAR 19.1307).
  • When the HUBZone preference does not apply: when price isn't a selection factor (for example, architect-engineer buys), when all fair and reasonable offers are accepted (for example, Multiple Award Schedule contracts), and on the reserved portion of a multiple-award solicitation (FAR 19.1307).

Example (illustrative), HUBZone on the open portion: a HUBZone firm offers $100,000 on the open CLINs. A large business offers $95,000. For evaluation only, the large offer becomes $95,000 × 1.10 = $104,500, so the HUBZone offer is evaluated as lower. If the evaluated prices tie, FAR 19.1307 says the HUBZone small business gets the award.

If you aren't HUBZone-certified, plan on competing purely on price and technical merit for the open portion. Don't price as though you'll get a discount that doesn't exist.

How to Decide Your Bid Strategy: Total vs Partial Set-Aside Checklist

Before you bid, confirm the set-aside type, your size under the assigned NAICS code, and whether your self-performance clears the subcontracting cap. Then decide which portions to price.

Step-by-step on SAM.gov

  1. Go to SAM.gov and choose Search, then the Contract Opportunities domain.
  2. In Filters, open Set Aside and select Total Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5) and/or Partial Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5). Add your codes under NAICS Code.
  3. Open a notice. In General Information, check Contract Opportunity Type: is it a Sources Sought, a Presolicitation, or a Solicitation? In Classification, check the Set Aside and NAICS Code fields.
  4. Open the SBA Size Standards Tool, enter that NAICS code, and confirm you're under the receipts or employee limit, counting affiliates.
  5. Download the solicitation attachments. For a partial set-aside, find the CLINs marked set aside and not set aside, plus the submission instructions (FAR 19.502-3(b)–(c)).
  6. Search the document for "52.219-14" and "52.219-7". Note which clause dates are cited and whether any "(DEVIATION)" labels appear.
  7. Build a subcontracting worksheet that lists every planned sub, marks each one similarly situated or not, and shows the dollars paid per period. Confirm you stay under 50%, 85% or 75%.
  8. Choose your play using the decision checklist below.

Decision checklist

  • Not small under the solicitation's NAICS code? Don't bid on a total set-aside or on the reserved portion. On a partial set-aside you may still bid on the open portion.
  • Small, but you'd need subcontractors that aren't similarly situated for more than half the work? Look for a similarly situated teammate, change your staffing, or don't bid on the prime. You could offer to subcontract to another small prime instead.
  • Total set-aside, and you can perform at least half yourself? It's usually your strongest field, so prioritize it.
  • Partial set-aside, with capacity only for the reserved portion? Price the reserved CLINs carefully, since that's where your competition is limited.
  • Partial set-aside, and you can handle both portions? Submit both if the instructions allow it. If your open-portion price isn't competitive, it shouldn't affect your reserved-portion offer, so check whether the solicitation evaluates the portions separately.
  • HUBZone-certified? Take a harder look at the open portion, where the 10% evaluation factor may apply.

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeFix
Bidding under your company's "usual" NAICS codeSize is judged against the NAICS code in the solicitation (13 CFR 121.404)
Counting a teammate's hours instead of dollars paidThe limit is based on the amount the government pays you (FAR 52.219-14)
Missing a size protest window against a competitorFive business days after you're notified of the apparent awardee in negotiated buys (13 CFR 121.1004)
Expecting a small business price discount on partial set-asidesOnly the HUBZone preference exists, in full and open competition (FAR 19.1307)

Can a Large Business Bid on a Partial Set-Aside?

Yes, but only on the non-reserved portion. A large business's offer on the reserved portion is treated as nonresponsive and rejected (FAR 19.502-3(d)).

Before rejecting an otherwise eligible offer over a question about the offeror's size, the CO has to get an SBA size determination (FAR 19.502-3(d)). For small bidders, this means a large competitor can win the open CLINs while you win the reserved ones. The government may then manage two contractors on related work.

Example (illustrative): on the 10-CLIN supply buy above, a large manufacturer wins CLINs 0001–0006 and a small distributor wins CLINs 0007–0010. The large firm would have been rejected if it had offered on 0007–0010.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Pitfall (for small firms): assuming large primes will team with you on the reserved portion. Fix: a large firm can only be your subcontractor there, and the dollars you pay it count against your 50% cap.
  • Pitfall (for growing firms): your size may change between proposals. Fix: re-check your size for each solicitation, because it's measured on the date of your initial offer with price (13 CFR 121.404).

Next steps

You can do the first three steps today on your own. If you'd like help, there are free options and paid ones.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Save a SAM.gov search with Set Aside filtered to SBA and SBP and your two or three main NAICS codes.
  2. Run the SBA Size Standards Tool for each of those NAICS codes and write down where you stand against each limit.
  3. Make a one-page subcontracting worksheet template with columns for subcontractor, similarly situated (Y/N), dollars per base or option period, and percent of the total. Reuse it on every bid.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) are funded through the DoD Office of Small Business Programs. They offer one-on-one counseling, SAM.gov registration help and bid matching, and most services cost nothing (as of October 2026; check the National APEX Accelerator Alliance). Good fit: first-time bidders who need help with registration and finding opportunities. Not a good fit: firms that need legal advice on a protest or a compliance dispute. Counselors aren't your attorneys, and their availability depends on your local center.
  • A government contracts attorney is the right call for size protests, GAO protests or questions about subcontracting compliance. Attorneys usually bill by the hour, and rates vary widely, so get a written estimate first. Not a good fit if you just need help finding bids, because that's expensive for routine work.

Related guide on this site:

  • Capability Statement Example: 5 Sections Buyers Read First. Use it when you answer the Sources Sought notices that decide whether a buy is set aside at all.

FAQ

What happens if a small business fails the rule of two after award?

The rule of two is the CO's expectation before the solicitation goes out, so it isn't retested after award. What matters after award is your size as of the date of your initial offer with price, and that generally holds for the life of the contract (13 CFR 121.404). If too few acceptable small business offers come in before award, the CO can withdraw the set-aside and resolicit it (FAR 19.502-2).

Can a set-aside be challenged or protested?

Yes. You can challenge the set-aside decision itself at GAO as a solicitation problem, and you must file before the closing date (4 CFR 21.2(a)(1)). You can also challenge a competitor's size by filing a size protest with the CO within five business days after you're notified of the apparent awardee in a negotiated procurement (13 CFR 121.1004).

Does a partial set-aside count as two separate contracts?

Not necessarily. It's one solicitation with portions that are set aside and portions that aren't, and depending on who wins, it can produce one award or several. FAR 52.219-7 lets offerors submit separate offers for each portion or one combined offer (FAR 52.219-7). The solicitation's instructions decide how the portions are evaluated and awarded.

What size standard applies to determine small business status?

The SBA size standard for the NAICS code the CO assigned to that solicitation applies. Depending on the industry, it's measured by average annual receipts or by number of employees, and it includes affiliates (SBA size standards). You must meet it on the date you submit your initial offer with price (13 CFR 121.404).
